Expedient

/ik-SPEE-dee-uhnt/ - the stress falls on SPEE · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Expedient means convenient and advantageous for oneself, putting practicality ahead of principle.

Trading the star pitcher felt expedient at the deadline — the payroll shrank, the owners cheered, and the fans paid for it all September.

Worked Example

Offered a way out of a scheduling crunch, the network made the expedient call: it aired the finale unfinished, visual effects and all, to beat a rival's premiere. Ratings won the night; the apology, the patched rerun, and the animators' resignations filled the month that followed.

Expedient is the exact word because it means convenient and advantageous, especially when serving one's own interest — the choice that works right now, with the cost quietly shipped to later or to someone else. Practical solves the problem; expedient serves the chooser, and the word usually arrives with an eyebrow raised.

How Expedient Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

convenient

convenient: easy and suitable, with no shadow over it

self-serving

self-serving: names the interest outright, and drops the practicality

Antonyms

upright

upright: choosing by principle even at a cost

honorable

honorable: the reputation earned by refusing shortcuts

How Strong Is It? — sensible → expedient → ruthless

sensible vs. expedient

sensible vs. expedient: Sensible is the honest cousin — the choice that simply works, with nothing traded away to get it.

ruthless vs. expedient

ruthless vs. expedient: Ruthless goes further than expedient — the expedient choice bends a principle for advantage; the ruthless one tramples people and never looks down.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: out, free

Root — -ped-

Root — -ped-: foot (Latin pes, pedis)

Suffix — -ient

Suffix — -ient: adjective ending: doing

Put it together

Put it together: Ex- (out, free) + -ped- (foot) + -ient (adjective ending) = getting the foot out. Latin expedire meant freeing a snared foot, and so doing whatever gets you moving again. The word remembers the snare: an expedient choice frees your foot fast, wherever the trap lands next.

Use the root in a new word: pedestrian

Use the root in a new word: pedestrian: A pedestrian travels on foot — the same ped- that expedient frees from the trap.

Root Check

Word Choice

critical / political

Expedient grades a choice by convenience rather than principle, so it carries a raised eyebrow — editorials love it. Beside its unit-mates: prudence weighs long-term consequences, where expedient dodges them; facile is the lazy argument, expedient the lazy ethics. When no self-interest shades the choice, plain convenient is the honest label.
